speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I'm Dr. Agent. Can you tell me exactly where the wrist pain is located and describe the appearance of the skin lesions you mentioned?

speaker: Patient
text: 17-year-old male. The patient presents with a 3-day history of pain in his left wrist, which worsened this morning accompanied by chills and malaise. He recounts having a self-resolving left knee pain the previous week. Reports recent return from a camping trip in Minnesota. Sexually active with one female partner. No history of trauma to the wrist.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given your recent camping trip in Minnesota, have you noticed any expanding red rash or a "bull's-eye" lesion on your skin? Also, can you confirm if you've seen or felt a tick bite recently?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Pain in the left wrist. I also have Chills, Malaise, Painless violaceous vesiculopustular lesions on both wrists and hands, Swelling and erythema of the left wrist, Severe tenderness to palpation and passive movement of the left wrist.

speaker: Doctor
text:
The description of painless violaceous vesiculopustular lesions on the hands and wrists, combined with your recent camping history in Minnesota and migratory joint pain, is highly suggestive of Sporotrichosis or potentially a specific tick-borne illness, but the skin findings are quite distinct. Do you have any history of exposure to cats, moss, or sphagnum peat moss during your camping trip?

REQUEST TEST: Fungal culture of skin lesion

speaker: Doctor
text:
The fungal culture results are normal, which effectively rules out Sporotrichosis. Given the camping history in Minnesota and the specific skin lesions, we need to consider other tick-borne illnesses like Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever or Ehrlichiosis. Have you experienced any severe headache, nausea, or sensitivity to light?

REQUEST TEST: Tick-borne disease panel (RMSF, Ehrlichia, Lyme)

speaker: Doctor
text:
The negative tick-borne panel and fungal culture are crucial clues, as the combination of migratory arthritis and painless violaceous vesiculopustular lesions on the hands is classic for disseminated gonococcal infection. Are you experiencing any pain or discharge with urination?

REQUEST TEST: Nucleic acid amplification test for Neisseria gonorrhoeae

speaker: Doctor
text:
The positive NAAT for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, combined with your migratory arthritis and characteristic skin lesions, confirms the diagnosis of disseminated gonococcal infection.

DIAGNOSIS READY: Disseminated Gonococcal Infection
